old_digest: One wicket shall be pitched, as in Law 6, with a bowling stump opposite to it, at a distance of 22 yards. The bowling crease shall be in line with the bowling stump, and drawn according to Law 7. When there shall be less than five players on a side, bounds shall be placed 22 yards each in a line from the off and leg stump. The ball must be hit before the bounds to entitle the striker to a run, which run cannot be obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease. When the striker shall hit the ball, one of his feet must be on the ground, behind the popping crease, otherwise the umpire s ...
The side which goes in second shall follow their innings if they have scored 75 runs less than the opposite side.
new_digest: The side which bats first and leads by 75 runs shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their innings.

old_digest: Prior to the commencement of a match it may be agreed that the over consist of five or six balls.
new_digest: Prior to the commencement of a match it may be agreed :—that the Over consist of 5 or 6 balls.
N.B.—A tie is included in the words “played out.”

old_digest: Prior to the commencement of a match it may be agreed that the over consist of five or six balls.

new_digest: One Wicket shall be pitched, as in Law 6, with a Bowling Stump opposite to it, at a distance of twenty-two yards. The Bowling crease shall be in a line with the bowling stump; and drawn according to Law 7. When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the off and leg stump. 16 The ball must be hit before the Bounds to entitle the Striker to a run, which run cannot be obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease. When the Striker shall hit the ball, one of his feet must be on the ground behind the popping crease, ot ...

old_digest: One wicket shall be pitched, as in Law 6, with a bowling stump opposite to it, at a distance of 22 yards. The bowling crease shall be in line with the bowling stump, and drawn according to Law 7.
new_digest: One Wicket shall be pitched, as in Law 6, with a Bowling Stump opposite to it, at a distance of twenty-two yards. The Bowling crease shall be in a line with the bowling stump; and drawn according to Law 7.

old_digest: There shall be no restriction as to the ball being bowled in overs, but no more than one minute shall be allowed between each ball.
new_digest: There shall be no restriction as to the ball being bowled in Overs, but no more than one minute shall be allowed between each ball.

old_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, bounds shall be placed 22 yards each in a line from the off and leg stump.
new_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the off and leg stump. 16

old_digest: The ball must be hit before the bounds to entitle the striker to a run, which run cannot be obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease.
new_digest: The ball must be hit before the Bounds to entitle the Striker to a run, which run cannot be obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease.

old_digest: When the striker shall hit the ball, one of his feet must be on the ground, behind the popping crease, otherwise the umpire shall call “no hit,” and no run shall be scored.
new_digest: When the Striker shall hit the ball, one of his feet must be on the ground behind the popping crease, otherwise the Umpire shall call “No Hit,” and no run shall be scored.

old_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, neither byes, leg-byes, nor overthrows shall be allowed, nor shall the striker be caught out behind the wicket, nor stumped.
new_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, neither Byes, Leg Byes, nor Overthrows shall be allowed, nor shall the Striker be caught out behind the wicket, nor stumped.

old_digest: The fieldsman must return the ball so that it shall cross the ground between the wicket and the bowling stump, or between the bowling stump and the bounds.
new_digest: The fieldsman must return the ball so that it shall cross the ground between the wicket and the bowling stump, or between the bowling stump and the bounds; the Striker may run till the ball be so returned.

old_digest: After the striker shall have made one run, if he starts again he must touch the middle stump or crease, and turn before the ball cross the ground to entitle him to another.
new_digest: After the Striker shall have made one run, if he start again he must touch the bowling stump or crease, and turn before the ball cross the ground to entitle him to another.

old_digest: The striker shall be entitled to three runs for lost ball, and the same number for ball wilfully stopped by a field-man otherwise than with any part of his person.
new_digest: The Striker shall be entitled to three runs for lost ball, and the same number for ball wilfully stopped by a fieldsman otherwise than with any part of his person.

old_digest: When there shall be more than four players on a side there shall be no bounds. All runs, byes, leg byes, and overthrows shall then be allowed.
new_digest: When there shall be more than four players on a side, there shall be no bounds. All Hits, Byes, Leg Byes, and Overthrows shall then be allowed.

old_digest: Each side has two innings, taken alternately, except in the case provided for in Law 53. A match is played between two sides of 11 players each, unless otherwise agreed to.
new_digest: A match is played between two sides of eleven players each, unless otherwise agreed to; each side has two innings, taken alternately, except in the case provided for in Law 53.

A bowler may bowl with both feet behind the bowling crease provided that one foot is within the return crease. If a bowler knock the wicket with his foot in delivering the ball and remove a bail, such act does not in itself justify an Umpire in calling “No Ball.” When part of the bowler’s foot is grounded on or outside the return crease the Umpire should call “No Ball.” Many bowlers deliver the ball with the toe of the back foot pointing towards the near wicket, and with the heel towards and over the return crease. If the bowler so delivers the ball with the heel on the ground, the Umpire “No Balls” him (the foot not being entirely within the return crease). If he delivers with the heel rais ...

The test for the Umpire to apply in deciding if the ball is wide is whether it is within reach of the Striker. If the striker hit a ball which has been called “Wide” the call should be ignored. When only one run has been made from a “Wide Ball” the batsmen do not cross over to the positions they were in before the run was made.

This Law should be read with Law 16. Though provision is made in Law 16 by which the Striker may obtain runs from a “No Ball” the fact remains that “neither a No Ball nor Wide Ball shall be reckoned as one of the over.” Although not counted in the over No Balls and Wides arc recorded in their proper place on the score sheet. It is Umpire’s and not the Scorer’s duty to call over.

old_digest: The bowler may change ends as often as he pleases, provided that he shall not bowl two overs in succession in the same innings.
new_digest: The Bowler shall be allowed to change ends as often as he pleases, provided only that he does not bowl two Overs consecutively in one innings.

old_digest: From a “wide ball” as many runs as are run shall be added to that score as “wide balls,” and if no runs be otherwise obtained, one run shall be so added.
new_digest: From a “Wide Ball” as many runs as are run shall be added to the score as “Wide Balls,” and if no run be otherwise obtained one run shall be so added. When a run is made by the bat off a “NoBall” only the run to the batsman should be scored and not the “No Ball” as well. If one run is attempted and the batsman is run out the “No Ball” alone counts. If runs are made off a “No Ball,” although the runs are scored and not the “No Ball,” the bowler is allowed another delivery. When Byes or Overthrows are run from a “Wide” they are scored as “Wides.” A Batsman may be out “hit wicket,” when striking at a “Wide.”

old_digest: If the ball, not having been called “wide” or “no-ball,” pass the striker without touching his bat or person, and any runs be obtained, the umpire shall call “bye;” but if the ball touch any part of the striker’s person (hand excepted) and any run be obtained, the umpire shall call “leg-bye;” such runs to be scored “byes” and “leg-byes” respectively.
new_digest: If the ball, not having been called “Wide” or “No Ball,” pass the Striker without touching his bat, or person, and any runs be obtained, the Umpire shall call “Bye”; but if the ball touch any part of the Striker’s person (hand excepted) and any run be obtained, the Umpire shall call “Leg Bye,” such runs to be scored “Byes” and “Leg Byes” respectively.

old_digest: No trial ball shall be allowed to any bowler on the ground between the wickets, and, when one of the batsmen is out the use of the bat shall not be allowed to any person until the next batsman shall come in. At the beginning of the match, and of each innings, the umpire at the bowler’s wicket shall call “play” from that time.
new_digest: At the beginning of the match, and of each innings, the Umpire at the Bowler’s wicket shall call “Play”; from that time no trial ball shall be allowed to any bowler on the ground between the wickets, and when one of the batsmen is out, the use of the bat shall not be allowed to any person until the next batsman shall come in.

It is sufficient if part of the batsman’s foot is grounded within the line. If the foot is on the line, but no part is within the batsman would be “out of his ground.” If the batsman is in the act of jumping in the air and the bat is also off the ground he would be “out of his ground.”

old_digest: A run is scored:— 1.—So often as the batsman after a hit, or at any time while the ball is in play, shall have crossed and made good their ground from end to end. 2.—For penalties under Laws 16, 34, 41, and allowances under 41.
new_digest: A run is scored:— 1st—So often as the Batsmen, after a hit, or at any time while the ball is in play, shall have crossed, and made good their ground from end to end. 2nd—For penalties under Laws 16, 34, 41, and allowances under 44.

When a batsman has actually made more runs for a boundary hit than have been arranged for the boundary, this Law will prevail, and the runs completed should be scored. Neither side can be compelled to continue after the match is finished. In a One Day Match the Umpires should decide if there is sufficient time left to carry the game to a further issue after each side has completed an innings.

If one bail is off it is sufficient to remove the remaining one with the ball in order to stump or run a batsman out. Although the Law says nothing about the stumps being pulled out it is customary to run a batsman out in this way when the bails are off; but the ball must be in the fieldsman’s hand when he uses it for this purpose.

old_digest: The striker is out if the wicket be bowled down, even if the ball first touch the striker's bat or person:
new_digest: If the wicket be bowled down, even if the ball first touch the Striker’s bat or person;—“ Bowled.” An Umpire would be justified in giving a batsman out “Bowled” if a stump were bowled down, but the bails by some mischance remained in position.

The ball must not touch the ground before it is held; but the hand holding the ball may touch the ground in effecting the catch. When a fieldsman catches a ball and falls and the ball touches the ground, it is a question of fact for the Umpire to decide whether or not the catch was completed before the ball touched the ground. When a Batsman plays a ball on to the ground and in order to prevent it hitting the wicket, after touching the ground, he strikes it again and the ball is caught, the batsman is not out. But if he hit the ball a second time before it touches the ground and is caught, he would be out under this Law. A Batsman would be out if caught off a ball which before striking the b ...

If the ball rebounds off the pads or person of the wicket-keeper, without having first touched the bat or hand of the Striker, and the Striker is out of his ground the decision should be “Stumped,” and not “Run Out.” It is sufficient for the wicket-keeper to remove one bail in order to run out or stump a batsman. It would not be out if he were to knock the bails off with his foot, or with an arm or hand not holding the ball.

old_digest: Or, if with any part of his person he stop the ball, which in the opinion of the umpire at the bowler's wicket shall have been pitched in a straight line from it to the striker's wicket and would have hit it:—“Leg before wicket.”
new_digest: Or, if with part of his person he stops the ball, which in the opinion of the Umpire at the bowler’s wicket, shall have been pitched in a straight line from it to the Striker’s wicket and would have hit it;—“Leg before wicket.” A Batsman may be out l.b.w. although the bowler is bowling round the wicket, if the case comes within this Law. There are three considerations which an Umpire must bear in mind:— (1) Would the ball have hit the wicket? (2) Did it pitch in a straight line between wicket and wicket? (3) Was it part of the batsman’s person which intercepted the ball? If these questions are answered in the affirmative the batsman would be out. It is immaterial whether the ball breaks or n ...

If in making a second stroke to keep a ball out of his wicket, the Striker hit down his wicket as above he would be out. A batsman would not be out for breaking the wicket either with his bat or person when in the act of running. If while playing at the ball, but not otherwise, the Striker’s hat or cap fell on the wicket and dislodged a bail he would be out.
It should be noted that it is the Striker who is out if this Law is infringed.

It is for the Umpire to decide whether the ball has been struck “wilfully” for some purpose other than that of guarding the wicket. The fact that a run is attempted may be evidence of the batsman’s intention to take advantage of the second stroke and the Umpire is entitled to regard it as such, but it is not conclusive. If the ball has been lawfully struck twice and an overthrow is made, the batsmen are entitled to the runs which follow. A Striker may be out for hitting the ball twice, although no run is attempted.

old_digest: Either batsman is out if in running, or at any other time, while the ball is in play, he be out of his ground, and his wicket be struck down by the ball after touching any fieldsman, or by the hand or arm (with ball in hand) of any fieldsman:—“Run out.”
new_digest: If in running, or at any other time, when the ball is in play he be out of his ground, and his wicket be struck down by the ball after touching any fieldsman, or by the hand or arm, with ball in hand, of any fieldsman;—“ Run out.” It would not be out if the striker hit the ball into the opposite wickets —the other batsman being out of his ground—unless the ball had been touched by a fieldsman after being hit and before striking the wickets. Either batsman can be “run out” at any time when the ball is in play by any fieldsman, including the bowler. For a definition of “out of his ground” see Law 19 and Notes.
It should be noted, especially in League and Saturday Matches, that Umpires are appointed “one for each end” and not one for each side.
The Umpire must decide on the facts before him if the obstruction was “wilful.”

(Sec Notes on Law 22.) Although that run which is being attempted shall not be scored it is not the custom for the remaining batsman to resume his position at the wicket he has left if he and his partner have crossed.

If the Ball, whether struck with the bat or not, lodges in a Batsman’s Clothing, the ball shall become “Dead.” A ball does not become “Dead” when the bails are off or the wickets struck down or because an unsuccessful appeal has been made. to the Umpire. Lodging in a batsman’s clothing includes practically all ways in which a ball can be said to lodge in or against his clothing. The ball does not become “Dead” on hitting the Umpire. The ball ceases to be “Dead” when the bowler begins his run or bowling action.

old_digest: If a ball in play cannot be found or recovered, any fieldsman may call “lost-ball,” when the ball shall be “dead;” six runs shall be added to the score; but if more than six runs have been run before “lost ball” has been called as many runs as have been run shall be scored.
new_digest: If a ball in play cannot be found or recovered, any Fieldsman may call “Lost Ball” when the ball shall be “Dead”; six runs shall be added to the score; but if more than six runs have been run before “Lost Ball” has been called, as many runs as have been run shall be scored. A ball can only become “Dead” under Laws 33a, 33b, 34, 35, 41 & 50, or on the call of a boundary hit.

old_digest: After the ball shall have been finally settled in the wicket keeper’s or bowler's hand, it shall be ‘dead;” but when the bowler is about to deliver the ball if the batsman at his wicket be out of his ground before actual delivery, the said bowler may run him out; but if the bowler throw at the wicket and any run result, it shall be scored “no ball.”
new_digest: After the ball shall have been finally settled in the Wicket-keeper’s or Bowler’s hand, it shall be “Dead”; but when the Bowler is about to deliver the ball, if the Batsman at his wicket be out of his ground before actual delivery, the said Bowler may run him out: but if the Bowler throw at that wicket and any run result, it shall be scored “No Ball.” Whether the ball is “finally settled” is a question of fact for the Umpire only to decide. A bowler may run a Batsman out, without having delivered the ball, in anyway authorized by the Laws, he may have passed the bowling crease in his run or may change the ball from one hand to the other before throwing at the wicket or knocking off the bails ...

old_digest: A substitute shall be allowed to field or run between wickets for any player who may, during the match be incapacitated from illness or injury, but for no other reason except with the consent of the opposite side.
new_digest: A substitute shall be allowed to field or run between wickets for any player, who may during the match, be incapacitated from illness or injury, but for no other reason, except with the consent of the opposite side. 13 It is well to remember that a side which loses a player’s services through illness or injury, brought about during a match, is entitled to a substitute, “it shall be allowed” whereas under other circumstances consent is necessary which must depend upon the courtesy of the opposing Captain. Many disputes would be avoided if the Captains, before tossing, exchanged lists of the players. There is no law prohibiting a player from bowling because he has had a substitute to run for h ...
The distinction between the words “Striker” and “Batsman” should be appreciated. When the injured Batsman is not the Striker he is subject to no penalty under this Law.

old_digest: It shall measure not less than nine inches, nor more than nine inches and one quarter in circumference.
new_digest: It shall measure not less than nine inches, nor more than nine inches and one-quarter in circumference. It has become the practice to call for a new ball at any time, with the Umpire’s consent, if the old one has become damaged or if the bowler has lifted the seam to obtain a better hold.

old_digest: A batsman is liable to be put out for any infringe ment of the laws by his substitute.
new_digest: A Batsman is liable to be out for any infringement of the Laws by his substitute.
The “five runs” are to be added to the runs already made when the Fieldsman “wilfully” stopped the ball.
A Wicket-keeper may run a Batsman out by going in front of the Wicket (Law 28) the Umpire must decide from the facts, if the act is legal.
(See also Instructions to Umpires.) 14

old_digest: When they call “play” the side refusing to play shall lose the match.
new_digest: When they shall call “Play” the side refusing to play shall lose the match. It is the duty of the Captains to see that this Law is strictly observed.
N.B.—An appeal, “How’s that?” covers all ways of being out (within the jurisdiction of the Umpire appealed to), unless a specific way of getting out is stated by the person asking.
When the Umpire at the bowler’s wicket has given a Batsman “not out” the other umpire may answer any appeal within his jurisdiction, subject to an observance of Law 50.

old_digest: The umpire shall take special care to call “no ball” instantly upon delivery; “wide ball” as soon as it shall have passed the striker.
new_digest: The Umpires shall take especial care to call “No Ball” instantly upon delivery; “Wide Ball” as soon as it shall have passed the striker. If an Umpire has called “No Ball” when the ball has not been delivered he should revoke his decision.

old_digest: The bat shall not exceed four inches and one-quarter in the widest part; it shall not be more than 38 inches in length.
new_digest: The Bat shall not exceed four inches and one-quarter in the widest part; it shall not be more than thirty-eight inches in length.
No act on the part of the fielding side can cause a batsman to be out after the Umpire has called “Over,” but an appeal may be made within the allotted time. 15

old_digest: No umpire shall be changed during a match unless with the consent of both sides, except in case of violation of Law 51, when either side may dismiss him.
new_digest: No Umpire shall be changed during a match, unless with the consent of both sides, except in case of violation of Law 51; then either side may dismiss him.

old_digest: The side which goes in second shall follow their innings if they have scored 150 runs less than the opposite side. 1.—On the last day of a match, or if a one day match at any time, the in-side shall be empowered to declare the innings at an end.
new_digest: The side which bats first and leads by 150 runs in a three days’ match, or by 100 runs in a two days’ match, shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their innings.

The In-side may declare their innings at an end in a three days’ match, at or after the luncheon interval on the second day; in a two days’ match on the second day, at any time; in a one day match at any time. (See also Instructions to Umpires as to “declaring.” A declaration of a first innings does not preclude a second innings. For the purpose of stating the result of a match, an innings declared at an end is regarded as completed and the victory, if accomplished, is in runs and not by wickets.

old_digest: The wickets shall be pitched opposite and parallel to each other at a distance of 22 yards. The Stumps shall be of equal and sufficient size to prevent the ball passing through, 27 inches out of the ground.
new_digest: The Wickets shall be pitched opposite and parallel to each other at a distance of twenty-two yards. The stumps shall be of equal and of sufficient size to prevent the ball from passing through, twenty-seven inches out of the ground.

old_digest: The bowling crease shall be in a line with the stumps 6 feet 8 inches in length, the stumps in the centre, with a return crease at each end, at right angles behind the wicket.
new_digest: The Bowling Crease shall be in a line with the stumps: six feet eight inches in length; the stumps in the centre; with a Return Crease at each end, at right angles behind the wicket. The Return Crease is shortened for convenience. It must be deemed unlimited in length. A proposal will come before the General Meeting of the M.C.C. in 1902, to increase the Bowling Crease to 8ft. 8in.

The batting side has a right to have the ground swept and rolled “for not more than 10 minutes” before the commencement of each innings and of each day’s play. It is the duty of the Captain to see that his side obtain this advantage.
